section.title: The Ark and the Death of Uzzah
section.sectionRationale: Fresh from his coronation and the capture of Jerusalem, David turns first to the ark of God, the throne of the LORD's presence that Israel had neglected since the days of Saul. His intentions are good and the whole assembly agrees, but the ark is carried on a new cart, Philistine style, rather than by the Levites on their shoulders as the Law required. When an ox stumbles, Uzzah reaches out to steady it and is struck down. The failed first attempt becomes a sober lesson in approaching God's holiness on His own terms, setting up the corrected, faithful procession of chapter 15.
section.thesis: Good intentions and popular enthusiasm are not enough when it comes to the things of God; the ark must be sought and carried His way, not by human convenience, and the sobering death of Uzzah teaches the post-exilic community, rebuilding worship from nothing, that the LORD's holiness cannot be handled carelessly, even by willing hands.
section.frameNote: Four beats: David proposes to bring back the ark, verses 1 to 4; the ark set on a new cart and the procession begins, verses 5 to 8; Uzzah reaches out and dies, verses 9 to 11; and David, now afraid, turns the ark aside to the house of Obed-edom, verses 12 to 14.

units.label: David proposes to bring back the ark
units.note: we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul

verses.text: Then David conferred with all his leaders, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds.

And he said to the whole assembly of Israel, “If it seems good to you, and if this is of the LORD our God, let us send word far and wide to the rest of our brothers in all the land of Israel, and also to the priests and Levites in their cities and pasturelands, so that they may join us.
Then let us bring back the {{aron|ark}} of our God, for we did not {{darash|inquire}} of Him in the days of Saul.”
And because this proposal seemed right to all the people, the whole assembly agreed to it.

units.label: The ark set on a new cart
units.note: carried Philistine style, not by the Levites

verses.text: So David assembled all Israel, from the River Shihor in Egypt to Lebo-hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim.
David and all Israel went up to Baalah of Judah (that is, Kiriath-jearim) to bring up from there the ark of God the LORD, who is enthroned between the cherubim, the ark that is called by the Name.
So they carried the ark of God from the house of Abinadab on a new cart, with Uzzah and Ahio guiding the cart.
David and all the Israelites were celebrating before God with all their might, with songs and on harps and lyres, with tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets.

units.label: Uzzah's death
units.note: the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah

verses.text: When they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark, because the oxen had stumbled.
And the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and He struck him down because he had put his hand on the ark. So he died there before God.
Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah. So he named that place {{parats|Perez-uzzah}}, as it is called to this day.

units.label: David fears God; the ark turns aside
units.note: how can I ever bring the ark of God to me

verses.text: That day David feared God and asked, “How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?”
So he did not move the ark with him to the City of David; instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
Thus the ark of God remained with the family of Obed-edom in his house for three months, and the LORD blessed his household and everything he owned.

aron.gloss: Ark or chest, here the ark of the covenant, the gold-covered box housing the tablets of the Law, over which the LORD was enthroned between the cherubim. It is the visible center of Israel's worship, and how it is approached is never a small matter.

darash.gloss: To inquire, seek, or consult. David admits Israel did not inquire of the ark, or of the LORD through it, in Saul's day, 10:14. The whole book of Chronicles contrasts kings who darash the LORD with those who do not; David's zeal to seek the ark here is genuine, even though the method he chooses is still mistaken.

parats.gloss: To break out, burst forth. The place is named Perez-uzzah, outbreak against Uzzah, from this root; the same root later names Perez, son of Judah and ancestor of David, born through an unexpected outbreak of grace, Genesis 38:29. Here the outbreak is judgment, a sobering reminder that God's holiness cannot be casually handled.

basic.context: David has just been crowned king over all Israel and has taken Jerusalem. His first great project is not a palace or an army but the ark of God, which had been neglected since Saul's reign. He gathers the whole nation with genuine enthusiasm to bring it home. But instead of following the Law, which required the Levites to carry the ark on their shoulders with poles, they put it on a new cart, the way the Philistines had once returned it, 1 Samuel 6:7. When an ox stumbles, Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark and is struck dead. David is angry and afraid, and the ark is turned aside to the house of Obed-edom rather than brought all the way to Jerusalem. The chapter raises hard questions: why would God kill a man who was only trying to help, and what does this teach about how we approach Him.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative with a sharp built-in lesson, made explicit later in 15:13, 'It was because you Levites were not with us the first time that the LORD our God burst forth in anger against us. For we did not consult Him about the proper order.' The problem was not Uzzah's heart alone but the whole nation's method: good enthusiasm dressed in the wrong obedience. God is not arbitrary here; He had given clear instructions in Numbers 4:15 and 7:9 that the ark must be carried by Kohathite Levites on their shoulders, under pain of death for touching it. David and the people simply had not asked.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on the ark, the aron, God's throne on earth, and on the fact that Israel did not darash, inquire or seek, the LORD about it in Saul's day, nor, it turns out, about the proper way to move it now. The place is named from parats, to burst or break out, the same root that later names Perez, the ancestor of David born through an unexpected act of grace; here the outbreak is judgment rather than blessing, a warning that must be heeded before the story can move toward its promised hope.
basic.typology: Uzzah's death anticipates the reality that no one can approach God's holiness on their own terms or by their own effort, however sincere. It points toward the need for a mediator who can bear the weight of God's presence safely to His people, a role only fulfilled in Christ, our great High Priest, who alone brings sinners into the presence of a holy God without them being destroyed.
basic.christ: Where Uzzah's well-meant touch brought death, Christ's own hands, pierced for us, bring life to all who come to God through Him. Hebrews 10 says we now have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, a new and living way that this scene shows was never available on human terms. The Law's demand that only consecrated Levites carry the ark, on pain of death, foreshadows that only the truly consecrated Priest could bring God's presence to His people without judgment falling.
basic.god: God is genuinely holy, and this is not a technicality; His presence is not a talisman to be handled by convenience or good intentions. Yet even in this hard chapter grace is present: the ark rests three months with Obed-edom and blesses his entire household, showing that nearness to God, sought rightly, is nothing but good.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 4:15 and 7:9 command that only the Kohathites carry the ark, by its poles, and never touch it directly. 1 Samuel 6:7 records the Philistines' cart method that Israel wrongly copies here. 1 Chronicles 15:13-15 states the lesson explicitly and corrects it.
basic.oneStory: This failed first attempt to bring the ark home teaches the returning exiles, and every reader, that God's presence must be sought on His terms, not ours. It is a dark hinge in the larger story of the ark coming to Jerusalem, preparing the way for the corrected, joyful procession of chapter 15 and, at last, for Christ, who opens access to God's presence for good.

context.literary:
The Chronicler tells this story with a compression that itself makes a point. Where 1 Samuel 4 to 7 devotes several chapters to the ark's capture, its plagues among the Philistines, its long exile at Kiriath-jearim, and Samuel's own leadership in those years, this chapter reduces all of that history to a single clause in David's mouth, 'we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul,' verse 3. The Chronicler is not interested in retelling Samuel's story; he is interested in David's choice, right now, at the very start of his reign as king over all Israel.

Notice, too, the scale the text insists on. David assembles Israel 'from the River Shihor in Egypt to Lebo-hamath,' verse 5, the same idealized, edge to edge borders used to describe the land's full extent in Joshua 13:3-5 and later in Solomon's kingdom, 2 Chronicles 9:26. This is meant to read as a whole nation, best foot forward undertaking, not a private or partial one, which is exactly why its failure carries such weight. Nothing about the intention is small or half hearted; the fault lies entirely in the method.

This is also David's first recorded act as king over the unified nation, coming immediately after the roll call of mighty men in chapters 11 to 12. The Chronicler positions worship, not war or building, as the new king's opening priority, a placement that will matter again when the corrected procession of chapter 15 takes up exactly this theme before any account of David's wars in chapters 18 to 20.
context.historical:
Uzzah and Ahio were, by the parallel account, sons of Abinadab, in whose house at Kiriath-jearim the ark had rested for some twenty years since its return from Philistine territory, 1 Samuel 7:1-2. They had grown up beside it. That long familiarity likely explains both the family's natural role in escorting it now and Uzzah's fatal, instinctive reach when the cart lurched, a reflex easier to understand in a man who had lived his whole life a few steps from the ark without incident.

Threshing floors, like the one at Chidon, sat on raised, open ground at the edge of a town, swept by wind for separating grain from chaff and used as common gathering space, which is likely why the procession passed through or near one on its route from Kiriath-jearim toward Jerusalem, a journey of roughly nine miles. The uneven, uncleared ground around such a site is exactly where a cart's wheel might catch and an ox stumble.

Moving valuables by ox cart was the ordinary technology of the ancient Near East, used for grain, tribute, even idols, as the Philistines themselves had used one to send the ark home a generation earlier, 1 Samuel 6:7-8. It was efficient and unremarkable, which is precisely the point: Israel borrowed a perfectly sensible pagan convenience for the one object in the world that was never meant to be handled by ordinary convenience at all.
context.canonical:
This is not the Bible's only story of sudden death at the start of a new work of God. Nadab and Abihu are struck down the very day the tabernacle's worship begins, for offering unauthorized fire the LORD had not commanded, Leviticus 10:1-3, a warning placed at the birth of Israel's whole sacrificial system much as Uzzah's death sits at the birth of Jerusalem's worship of the ark. Centuries later, at the founding moment of the church, Ananias and Sapphira fall dead for treating something entrusted to God's people as though it were an ordinary thing to manage on their own terms, Acts 5:1-11, and Luke records that great fear seized the whole assembly, the same effect Uzzah's death has on David, verse 12. Paul later warns the Corinthians that some among them had grown weak, and some had died, for approaching the Lord's Table carelessly, 1 Corinthians 11:29-30, still reckoning with the truth this chapter first states in blunt narrative form: nearness to what is holy is never safe to presume upon.

The naming itself, 'Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day,' verse 11, follows a pattern found across Israel's early history, where a place is renamed after a decisive divine act and the name itself becomes a permanent, public memorial, as with Bochim, Judges 2:5, or Bethel, Genesis 28:19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The Chronicler wrote for a community that had watched worship collapse entirely, exile, a burned temple, decades without ark or altar, and was now attempting to rebuild it with no living memory of how it once worked. For such readers, this chapter is not primarily a character study of Uzzah; it is a manual correction. The Chronicler wants the returned exiles to see, in vivid and costly detail, that reviving Israel's worship life is not simply a matter of restoring enthusiasm, singing again, gathering again, wanting God's presence again, but of restoring it along the specific lines God had already given through Moses. He places this failure immediately before the Levitical consecration and correct procedure of chapter 15 quite deliberately, so that his readers feel the cost of skipping the details before they read the model of getting them right. He also wants them to see that David himself, their ideal king, was capable of this exact mistake, so that no reader mistakes good leadership or sincere zeal alone as sufficient grounds for confidence that worship is being rightly ordered.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Nothing in this chapter instructs New Testament believers to expect that a mistake in worship procedure will bring sudden physical death, and no church today carries a box with literal poles to obey. Those Mosaic specifics belonged to Israel's covenant arrangement and to the ark's unique role as the LORD's earthly throne; they are not a transferable ritual code. What does transfer, because the New Testament itself draws a similar line from other episodes of careless handling of holy things, Acts 5 and 1 Corinthians 11 among them, is the underlying principle: God's presence and God's appointed means of approach are not incidental details to be improved upon by human efficiency. Reading verse 10 as a timeless threat against clumsy churchgoers misses the text; reading it as evidence that God takes the manner of approaching Him seriously, and always has, gets the application right.

debates.question: Was Uzzah's death disproportionate to his fault?

views.label: A necessary, exemplary judgment
views.case: Uzzah, whether or not he was a Kohathite Levite, had grown too familiar with a sacred object he had lived beside for years, 1 Samuel 7:1-2; his reflex to touch the ark, though instinctive, exposed a deeper carelessness about God's explicit command, and the severity of the judgment matched the seriousness with which God had always treated unauthorized contact with holy things, as with Nadab and Abihu in Leviticus 10:1-3.

views.label: A judgment primarily on the nation's method, focused on Uzzah as its representative
views.case: The Chronicler's own commentary in 15:13 places the blame squarely on the whole nation's failure to consult the LORD about the proper order, not merely on Uzzah personally; Uzzah's death functions as a public, unforgettable object lesson that stops the entire procession and forces David and Israel to relearn how God must be worshiped.

debates.bearing: Either way, the text does not present God as capricious; it presents Him as unfailingly holy, and the whole nation, not Uzzah alone, needed correcting, which is exactly what happens by chapter 15.

debates.question: Was David wrong to be angry at the LORD in verse 11?

views.label: A sinful, self-focused anger
views.case: David's anger seems to protest God's judgment rather than examine his own failure to consult the Law, an understandable but flawed human reaction to being confronted with his own carelessness in worship.

views.label: A raw, honest grief that quickly turns to godly fear
views.case: The text moves seamlessly from David's anger, verse 11, to his fear of God, verse 12, suggesting a man wrestling honestly with a terrifying event before arriving, within the same day, at humble, corrected reverence, precisely the response the Chronicler commends over pretending nothing happened.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that David's anger gives way immediately to appropriate fear and caution, verses 12 to 13, modeling a right response to being confronted with one's own failure before God.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond aron, darash, and parats, the chapter is dense with words worth pausing over.

David 'conferred' with his leaders, verse 1, from ya'ats, the same root that gives counsel throughout Israel's wisdom literature, Proverbs 15:22, and that describes Ahithophel's fateful advice to David's son later, 2 Samuel 16:23. It is a strong word for careful, deliberate consultation, which makes the chapter's outcome so pointed: David consults his commanders and the whole qahal, assembly or congregation, verse 2, a word for Israel gathered as one covenant body, used already for the assembly Moses addressed, Numbers 20:4, and later for the assembly gathered at the temple's dedication, 2 Chronicles 6:3. He consults nearly everyone except, it turns out, the Law itself.

Verse 6 says the ark is 'called by the Name,' or more literally that the Name, ha-shem, is called over it. Attaching God's own personal name to an object marks it as uniquely His, the same idiom used of the city and temple called by His Name, Jeremiah 7:10-11, and of Israel itself, called by His name, Deuteronomy 28:10. The ark is not a national relic but the place where the LORD has staked His own name and reputation.

The celebration in verse 8 uses forms of the root sachaq, play or make merry, the same root that describes Michal's contempt for David two chapters later in the parallel account, 2 Samuel 6:20-21, and the laughter Sarah names her son for, Genesis 21:6. It can describe innocent delight or, in other contexts, mockery; here it is unmixed joy, which makes its sudden interruption in verse 9 so jarring.

Finally, 'the anger of the LORD burned,' verse 10, uses charah, a verb pictured as heat kindling, paired in the wider idiom with aph, nose or nostrils, the seat of anger in Hebrew speech, as though wrath were visible breath. The same phrase describes God's anger at Israel's later idolatry, Exodus 32:10, and at Moses' own reluctance, Exodus 4:14, always marking a serious, not casual, breach. Even the site's later name, Perez-uzzah, keeps that seriousness fixed permanently onto the map, so that a passerby generations afterward would still be reminded, by the ground itself, that this was no minor lapse. Together these five roots, ya'ats, qahal, shem, sachaq, and charah, trace the whole arc of the chapter from careful counsel to unguarded joy to sudden, burning judgment.

typology.type: The ark, untouchable except by the consecrated who bear it rightly
typology.fulfillment: No hand, however willing, could touch the ark and live unless it belonged to a consecrated Levite carrying it by its poles, Numbers 4:15. That real but partial safety finds its full answer in Jesus, our great High Priest, who alone is fit to carry God's presence to sinners without their being destroyed, and who has opened access to the Most Holy Place itself through His own blood, Hebrews 10:19-20. The type falls short because the Levites' preparation only ever permitted safe distance from the ark; Jesus abolishes the distance altogether, seating believers in the heavenly realms with Him, Ephesians 2:6.

typology.type: Uzzah struck down for reaching out to steady what was toppling
typology.fulfillment: Uzzah's death shows that even an instinctive, well meant touch cannot avert God's holiness on human terms; judgment fell the moment unauthorized hands met the ark. At the cross this pattern is reversed rather than repeated: instead of judgment falling on hands that reach toward God, it falls on the Son who reaches toward sinners, bearing the judgment His own holiness required so that those who now reach toward Him in faith are welcomed rather than struck down, 1 Timothy 2:5-6, Romans 3:25-26. The escalation is total: what killed Uzzah gives life to everyone found in Him.

typology.type: The blessing that spread to Obed-edom's household simply because the ark rested there
typology.fulfillment: For three months an ordinary household experienced tangible favor for no reason but the ark's nearby presence, verse 14, a foretaste that mere proximity to God is never wasted, even just after a frightening episode nearby. The New Testament escalates this from temporary proximity to permanent indwelling: believers themselves become the dwelling place of the Spirit, 1 Corinthians 3:16, and every blessing in the heavenly realms comes to them not because an ark rests near their house but because the Spirit now lives within them, Ephesians 1:3. The shadow of borrowed nearby blessing becomes the substance of a blessing that is owned and permanent.

study.christ:
This chapter reaches toward Christ first by exposing exactly what stands in the way of any sinner drawing near to a holy God: not merely disobedience in general, but the absence of a mediator fit to bear that nearness safely. David assembles the whole nation, secures full agreement, and still cannot bring the ark home, because willing hearts and popular consensus were never the qualification God required. Only consecrated hands, carrying by the appointed means, could do that safely, and even they were merely permitted proximity, not full access. The chapter therefore leaves a gap that the rest of Scripture keeps pressing toward: someone must come who does not merely carry God's presence at a careful distance but brings it near without any danger at all.

Hebrews answers that gap directly. The blood of bulls and goats, and even the careful poles of the Kohathites, could never do more than manage the danger of God's holiness; they could not remove it. Jesus does what neither ritual distance nor sincere zeal could achieve: by one sacrifice He has made perfect forever those who are being sanctified, Hebrews 10:14, and through His own torn flesh He has opened for us a new and living way into the Most Holy Place itself, Hebrews 10:19-20. Where the old system's answer to holiness was distance, carefully measured and enforced by death, His answer is nearness, freely given and secured by His own death instead of ours.

There is a pointed contrast worth sitting with. Uzzah reached toward the ark to keep the throne of God's presence from falling, and death met his hand. Jesus reaches toward fallen, guilty people, and life meets theirs. The direction of the rescue is reversed entirely: it is no longer a man's hand steadying a holy throne, but a pierced hand steadying man. Paul can therefore say what would have been unthinkable at Kiriath-jearim, that believers may approach the throne of grace with confidence, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need, Hebrews 4:16.

None of this cancels the chapter's warning. The New Testament does not soften the seriousness of approaching a holy God on our own terms; it relocates the danger onto the Savior Himself at the cross, so that those who come to Him no longer meet the anger that burned against Uzzah, but peace instead, Romans 5:1. The mediator this chapter shows Israel still needed, and did not yet have, is finally supplied, and supplied at great cost.
study.god:
This chapter will not let readers domesticate holiness into a manageable idea. The LORD is not honored simply because a nation wants Him near, sings joyfully, or musters full consensus; all of that is present here, verses 4 and 8, and it is not enough. His holiness has content, specific, revealed content, given generations earlier through Moses, and ignoring that content, however unintentionally, provokes the same real anger that outright rebellion would. The text does not soften this into metaphor. 'The anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and He struck him down,' verse 10, is reported as plainly as any other event in the chapter, without apology or qualification.

Yet the chapter refuses a purely fearsome portrait as well. Notice what does not happen: David, whose plan this was, and the priests and leaders who agreed to it, and the crowds singing and dancing in verse 8 are not struck. Judgment falls with precision on one specific act of unauthorized contact, not on the nation's general enthusiasm, which the LORD had, after all, inspired. This is a God who distinguishes carefully between sincere zeal directed wrongly and outright contempt, even while He will not simply overlook a wrong method for the sake of a right heart behind it.

Then, almost as an aside, verse 14 records that the LORD blessed Obed-edom's household and everything he owned during the very three months the ark sat, unplanned and unglamorous, in his house. This is easy to read past, but it is a remarkable claim: the same holiness that struck one man down pours out ordinary, tangible blessing on an ordinary household simply because the ark rested nearby and was not resisted. Holiness, in other words, is not merely a hazard to be minimized but a source of blessing to be rightly approached; the danger in this chapter was never nearness itself, but nearness attempted on the wrong terms.

Finally, the chapter shows a God who is patient with process. He does not demand David get everything right on the first attempt in order to remain gracious toward him; David is permitted to pause, reconsider, and try again, and the corrected procession of chapter 15 will succeed precisely because this failure was allowed to teach rather than to end the relationship.

crossReferences.note: The LORD's own instruction for the Kohathites: once the priests have finished covering the ark and the other holy furnishings, the Kohathites may come to carry them, but they must not touch the holy objects, or they will die. This is the specific command Israel bypasses at Chidon, not through malice but through simply never having asked what the Law required.

Moses gives the sons of Kohath no wagons at all, unlike the other Levitical clans who receive ox carts for the tabernacle's fabric and frames, because their duty was to carry the holy things on their shoulders. The absence of any cart provision for the ark's own carriers makes David's new cart, however innocently chosen, a departure from a decision God had made generations earlier.

The Philistines, wanting to be rid of the ark's plagues without understanding Israel's God, hitch two milk cows to a new cart and let it go, a pagan divination method meant to test whether their troubles truly came from the LORD. Israel unknowingly repeats the very method its enemies devised for a foreign god they did not know, rather than the method the true God had already revealed.

Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD on the very day Israel's sacrificial worship begins, and fire consumes them instantly. Moses' explanation to Aaron, that the LORD will show Himself holy among those who approach Him, reads like a commentary written in advance over Uzzah's death: sincerity and proximity to sacred office never substitute for doing exactly what God has said.

The fuller, near identical parallel account of this same failed procession, including additional detail about David's dance before the ark and his anger and fear afterward. Reading the two versions together shows how closely the Chronicler follows his source here, even while the surrounding chapters around it are freely rearranged for his own theological purposes.

David's own later diagnosis of exactly what went wrong: it was because the Levites were not with them the first time that the LORD burst forth in anger, for they did not consult Him about the proper order. The corrected procession that follows carries the ark on Levitical shoulders by its poles, precisely reversing chapter 13's fatal shortcut.

Ananias and Sapphira fall dead for lying about an offering entrusted to the young church's common life, and great fear seized the whole church and all who heard of these things, language that echoes the fear David feels after Uzzah's death, verse 12. Both scenes sit at the founding moment of a new stage of God's people's worship, and both teach the same costly lesson.

Because of Jesus' blood, believers now have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by a new and living way opened through His body, and are urged to draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith. What proved fatal for Uzzah on human initiative becomes, through the Savior's initiative alone, the safest and most welcomed approach any person can make.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 ends with cherubim barring the way back into Eden, guarding a holiness humanity had forfeited by distrust. Every subsequent stage of the story is, in one sense, the long labor of reopening that way without destroying the people who need it reopened. The tabernacle, and later the ark at its center, was Israel's provisional answer, a portable Eden, a throne pitched among a covenant people, hedged about with exact conditions for approach so that nearness would not simply repeat the first catastrophe. This chapter shows what happens when those conditions are forgotten even by people eager for God's presence and confident of their own good intentions: the ancient danger has not gone away just because centuries have passed and a king now wants Him near.

Positioned right after David's coronation and right before his palace and victories in chapter 14, this failure insists that no achievement of David's reign, however God given, can substitute for getting worship right; kingship, architecture, and military success are all downstream of whether Israel actually seeks the LORD on His own terms. The story does not let this failure be the last word. It moves at once toward correction, the consecrated Levites and joyful, careful procession of chapter 15, and then toward covenant, the everlasting promise to David's house in chapter 17, showing that the same LORD who struck down careless hands is building an unshakeable kingdom for the very family that just failed Him.

The whole trajectory answers, in the end, in the true meeting place of God and His people, in whom access to a holy God's presence is no longer mediated by careful poles and consecrated hands operating at safe distance, but by flesh and blood freely given so that the way into the Most Holy Place stands permanently open, Hebrews 10:19-20. What Genesis 3 barred and 1 Chronicles 13 shows still dangerous, Revelation 21:3 finally resolves: God's dwelling place with man, unguarded, unafraid, and everlasting.

quiz.q: Why did David want to bring the ark to Jerusalem?

options.text: Because Israel had neglected the ark and failed to inquire of the LORD through it in the days of Saul, and David wanted to restore it to the center of the nation's life.
options.note: Verse 3 gives David's own reasoning, tied to Saul's earlier unfaithfulness, 10:13-14.

options.text: Because he wanted a grand religious ceremony to celebrate his new throne.
options.note: David's motive was corporate worship and seeking the LORD, not mere royal display.

options.text: Because the ark was under threat from a foreign army.
options.note: No such threat is mentioned; the ark had simply been neglected since Saul's day.

options.text: Because the whole assembly agreed it seemed like a good and popular idea.
options.note: True, verse 4 records the assembly's agreement, but David's own stated reason was deeper, restoring what had been neglected under Saul.

quiz.q: What went wrong in how Israel moved the ark?

options.text: They carried it on a new cart, as the Philistines once had, instead of having the Levites carry it on their shoulders by its poles as the Law commanded.
options.note: Verse 7 and 15:13, 15 make explicit that the wrong method, not merely wrong hearts, caused the disaster.

options.text: They moved it at night without proper light.
options.note: Nothing in the text concerns timing or darkness; the failure was in the method of transport.

options.text: They used oxen instead of horses.
options.note: The animal was not the issue; the problem was that the ark rode on a cart at all rather than being carried by consecrated Levites.

options.text: They failed to have music and celebration during the procession.
options.note: Verse 8 shows there was abundant celebration; the failure was procedural, not a lack of joy or music.

quiz.q: Why did Uzzah die when he reached out to steady the ark?

options.text: Because he touched the ark directly, violating God's clear command that it could only be carried untouched by its poles, and the LORD's anger burned against this handling of His holiness.
options.note: Verses 9-10 record the act and the LORD's judgment; Numbers 4:15 forbids touching the holy things.

options.text: Because he was secretly an unfaithful man deserving death for unrelated sins.
options.note: The text gives no such background; the judgment falls specifically on his touching the ark.

options.text: Because the oxen had stumbled and he panicked.
options.note: The stumbling oxen explain his instinct to reach out, but the judgment fell because he touched the ark, not because he panicked.

options.text: Because he was not consecrated as a priest to make offerings.
options.note: Close, but the specific violation was touching the ark itself, which not even most Levites, let alone priests, were permitted to do; only the poles were to be carried.

quiz.q: How did David respond immediately after Uzzah's death?

options.text: He became angry and then afraid, and turned the ark aside to the house of Obed-edom instead of bringing it on to the City of David.
options.note: Verses 11-13 record both his anger and his fear, and the decision to leave the ark at Obed-edom's house.

options.text: He immediately corrected the Levites' carrying method and completed the journey to Jerusalem.
options.note: That correction only comes later, in chapter 15; here David turns the ark aside rather than continuing.

options.text: He ordered the ark destroyed as a dangerous object.
options.note: David never considers destroying the ark; he simply diverts it to safekeeping at Obed-edom's house.

options.text: He was afraid and set the ark aside, though the text does not record his anger.
options.note: True that he set it aside in fear, but this omits his recorded anger in verse 11, which precedes his fear.

quiz.q: What happened to Obed-edom's household while the ark stayed with him?

options.text: The LORD blessed his household and everything he owned during the three months the ark remained there.
options.note: Verse 14 records this blessing, a note of grace within a hard chapter.

options.text: His household suffered the same fate as Uzzah.
options.note: The opposite is true; his household was blessed, not judged.

options.text: Nothing in particular is recorded about his household.
options.note: The text specifically notes the LORD blessed his household, so this understates what is recorded.

options.text: He was required to become a Levite in order to keep the ark safely.
options.note: The text does not record such a requirement here; it simply notes the LORD's blessing on his household, though Obed-edom is later identified among the Levites, 15:18.

quiz.q: What is the chapter's abiding lesson for approaching God?

options.text: Sincere zeal for God's presence must still be joined to careful obedience to how He has said He is to be approached; good intentions do not replace His revealed way.
options.note: This is the Chronicler's own summary in 15:13, applied backward to this chapter's failure.

options.text: God does not care how His people worship as long as their hearts are sincere.
options.note: The whole episode shows the opposite; sincerity did not prevent judgment when God's revealed way was ignored.

options.text: Worship should always be celebratory and joyful above all else.
options.note: Celebration is present, verse 8, but it is not the chapter's main lesson; the failure was procedural, not a lack of joy.

options.text: Only priests, never ordinary worshipers, should ever be involved in moving sacred objects.
options.note: Close, since only consecrated Levites could carry the ark, but the chapter's deeper point is about obedience to God's revealed order generally, not merely priestly exclusivity.

questions: David's zeal to bring back the ark was genuine, yet the method was wrong. Where might you be pursuing God's presence or blessing with sincere enthusiasm but without carefully asking what His word actually says?
Uzzah's death is hard to read. How does remembering God's holiness, rather than assuming familiarity with sacred things, change the way you approach worship and prayer?

David's anger turned to fear, and fear led him to pause rather than push ahead. When have you needed to stop and reconsider a plan, even a well-meant one, in light of how God has actually asked to be honored?
Obed-edom's household was blessed simply by the ark's nearness, even after the tragedy. How does this shape your confidence that seeking God rightly, even after past mistakes, is never in vain?
This failed attempt sets up the corrected procession of chapter 15. Where in your own life might God be inviting you to try again, this time on His terms, after an earlier well-meaning failure?

translationNotes.note: The threshing floor is called Chidon here and Nacon in the parallel account, 2 Samuel 6:6; the BSB footnote treats Chidon as a variant name for the same site.
Perez-uzzah means outbreak against Uzzah, per the BSB footnote, from the same Hebrew root, parats, that later names Perez, ancestor of David, Genesis 38:29 and Ruth 4:12.
